item.description:
BANGLADESH is suffering the consequences of a Middle East war that continues to drag on, like many other countries dependent on imported energy. In June, QatarEnergy warned that it might ship only 20 of the 40 cargoes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) expected this year, and officials returned to buying gas through emergency tenders at higher prices. But this is only part of the story.

The war has exposed just how much of the country’s economic wellbeing depends on the Gulf. Three-quarters of the Bangladeshis who went abroad for work between FY2015 and FY2025 went to the Middle East, and close to half of the country’s remittances come from the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. This is the backdrop against which Dhaka is weighing the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed on August 7. Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman has already told parliament that the government would consider an invitation positively.

Whether Bangladesh should join at all is a separate debate. But if the government decides to align itself with Saudi Arabia, it has an opportunity to negotiate the terms before signing. Nothing should be given away for free: Bangladesh should leverage its alignment to secure commitments on its migrant workers, skills development, energy security and investment.

Of course, the obvious question is: why would Saudi Arabia listen? Because the Kingdom is building a coalition, and there is strength in numbers. The Pact’s signatories have said it is open to other states. Bangladesh has already joined a Saudi-led maritime alliance of 14 countries covering the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and on September 2, its defence adviser discussed expanded military training exchanges and disaster management cooperation with the Saudi ambassador. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected to travel to Riyadh at the crown prince’s invitation. A country that is being courted has bargaining power, and that power is greatest before it signs. Once the ink is dry, every request becomes a favour.

The very first ask should be to secure the livelihoods of one of Bangladesh’s most valuable economic assets: its migrant workforce. According to BMET, more than 9.69 lakh Bangladeshis left for overseas jobs in FY2025 -26, the lowest figure in five years. Recruiters say Saudi Arabia is now the only market in the Middle East that is still actively hiring, but that landscape is rapidly shifting. The Kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund has dropped large-scale projects from its 2026-30 strategy and cut some project budgets by up to 60 percent, while growth in the number of registered construction workers in the Kingdom slowed from 32 percent in 2025 to 6 percent in the first quarter of 2026.

A World Bank study found that more than 60 percent of Bangladeshi migrants abroad work in construction, putting the country’s workers—and a major source of foreign remittances—at risk. The employment agreement the two countries signed in October 2025, which promised stronger protections, guaranteed wages and better welfare, needs to be backed by firm targets and a clear pathway for skilled workers.

Protecting these jobs, however, requires more than baseline quotas; it demands a joint commitment to upskilling. Saudi Arabia now requires low-skilled foreign workers to pass its Takamul skill verification before they can be hired, and in October 2025, as the requirement took hold, departures from Bangladesh fell by 18.46 percent. Bangladesh now tests roughly 60,000 workers each month across 28 centres. That is progress, but the cost of meeting Riyadh’s standards falls largely on the workers themselves, who pay about $50 for each test, while the state pays for training programmes to prepare them.

If the Kingdom wants skilled labour, it should share that cost. The October 2025 agreement already bars agencies and employers from charging workers unauthorised fees; extending that principle to testing fees, while co-funding training and testing centres in Bangladesh, would be a modest next step. But the real payoff lies beyond construction sites. As the Gulf races to build data centres and cloud infrastructure, it needs network engineers and IT technicians. A joint digital skills initiative could finally help move Bangladeshi workers beyond predominantly manual labour and into higher-skilled, higher-earning occupations.

Beyond labour, Dhaka’s most pressing domestic vulnerability remains its energy sector. This year has shown how little protection Bangladesh’s long-term gas contracts can offer when supplies come under pressure. Dhaka has now secured $3.3 billion in financing from the Jeddah-based International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation to pay for fuel, gas and fertiliser this fiscal year.

Saudi Arabia does not sell gas to Bangladesh, but Saudi Aramco supplies crude oil to the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC), and the Kingdom is the largest shareholder in the Islamic Development Bank Group, of which the trade finance corporation is part. A deferred-payment facility for oil imports and access to cheaper Islamic trade finance could do more to strengthen Bangladesh’s energy security than almost any diplomatic gesture.

Whatever terms it secures in Riyadh, Dhaka must also protect what it already has elsewhere in the Gulf. More than a million Bangladeshis live in the UAE. Visa processing for most categories of Bangladeshi applicants has been effectively frozen since 2024, while remittances from the UAE fell by more than 10 percent in 2025, to $4.16 billion. The Makkah Pact has also drawn criticism from prominent commentators in the UAE, giving Bangladesh another reason to tread carefully.

The government has so far played down concerns about how joining the pact might affect relations with other states. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has described the expanded pact as an internal Muslim matter carrying no foreign policy risk, maintaining that there is no reason for concern. That may be good diplomatic messaging, but it is not a strategy.

Moving closer to Riyadh requires Bangladesh to pursue parallel diplomatic tracks across the Gulf to safeguard its migrant workforce and broader economic interests. Dhaka should consider putting forward similar strategic asks to Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and the UAE, with the normalisation of visa processing in the UAE as an immediate priority. Crucially, these relationships—along with vital gas supplies from Qatar and Oman—must not become collateral damage in any new arrangement with Riyadh.

None of these demands is unreasonable given what Bangladesh has already contributed to the Gulf. For decades, Bangladeshi workers have poured the concrete that built its cities, often in punishing heat and for modest wages, while sending home the remittances that have helped carry their own country through one economic shock after another. If Bangladesh is now prepared to offer Saudi Arabia its political alignment as well, it should make sure that alignment advances its own national interests.

Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

item.title: Can the RMG sector maintain its position in the global apparel market?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry stands at a critical juncture. The sector generates over 80% of the country’s export earnings while supporting millions of livelihoods. However, global competitiveness now extends beyond cost, quality, and delivery to include sustainability, transparency, responsible business practices, and credible environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance.
The key question is whether Bangladesh can move beyond a compliance-driven mindset and leverage sustainability practices and reporting as strategic tools to strengthen its position in the global apparel market.
The RMG sector transformed significantly after the 2013 Rana Plaza tragedy, which exposed critical weaknesses in workplace safety, labour compliance, and factory governance. In response, the industry adopted widespread reforms supported by global initiatives, regulatory authorities, and international buyers.
These reforms led to significant improvements in workplace safety, structural integrity, labour standards, and environmental management. Bangladesh now hosts the world’s largest number of LEED-certified green garment factories. Many manufacturers have also adopted energy-efficient technologies, wastewater treatment, water recycling, and renewable energy systems, demonstrating the sector’s growing commitment to sustainable manufacturing.
Despite these achievements, Bangladesh operates in an increasingly competitive global apparel market. Increasing competition from Vietnam, India, and Turkey highlights the need to strengthen competitiveness beyond low-cost production. Future success will depend on sustainability performance, innovation, supply-chain transparency, and resilience rather than price alone.
Global sustainability transformation requires organizations to integrate sustainability practices with credible sustainability reporting through a structured five-step roadmap. The process begins with assessment and governance, where organizations identify material ESG risks using double materiality and align priorities with the UN SDGs.
Photo: Courtesy
Next, sustainability is embedded into operations through carbon measurement, Scope 3 emissions management, renewable energy, circular production, labour rights, and supply chain traceability.
These practices respond to evolving global regulations. The roadmap then focuses on performance monitoring using measurable ESG indicators and science-based climate targets (SBTi). Finally, organizations disclose sustainability performance through frameworks such as GRI and SASB supported by external assurance.
Together, sustainability practices and reporting enhance accountability, market access, investor confidence, and the long-term competitiveness of Bangladesh’s RMG sector.
Over the past two decades, sustainability has become a core requirement in global apparel supply chains. International brands increasingly require compliance with standards on labour rights, occupational safety, environmental management, and responsible sourcing.
Frameworks such as GRI, the Higg Index, and ZDHC have accelerated the adoption of cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, resource-efficient production, and stronger monitoring systems across factories. Industry leaders increasingly recognize that long-term competitiveness depends not only on compliance but also on embedding sustainability into core business strategy.
A key pillar of this transformation is sustainability reporting. Leading Bangladeshi manufacturers have begun publishing sustainability and ESG reports using internationally recognized frameworks. These early adopters reflect growing alignment with global expectations and increasing institutional maturity across the sector.
Sustainability reporting strengthens buyer confidence, improves operational efficiency, supports access to green finance, and enhances risk management. It also enables manufacturers to benchmark performance and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.
However, progress remains uneven across the industry. While large exporters are increasingly adopting structured reporting, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still lack the technical expertise, financial resources, and data management systems needed for comprehensive reporting.
As a result, they continue to rely on fragmented disclosures driven by buyer audits, certifications, and compliance requirements.
This gap reduces transparency, limits comparability, and raises concerns about data reliability across the value chain.
Although sustainability reporting is not yet mandatory for all manufacturers, it is expected to become a formal requirement by 2027 as global regulatory frameworks evolve.
Bridging this gap will require coordinated efforts to strengthen technical capacity, improve digital infrastructure, and expand access to affordable green finance.
Despite significant progress, several structural challenges continue to limit the full sustainability transformation of Bangladesh’s RMG industry.
One major challenge is the sector’s continued reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy systems, which restricts large-scale emissions reduction. Although some factories have adopted renewable energy solutions, the national energy structure remains carbon intensive.
Access to green finance is another key constraint, especially for SMEs investing in cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, and digital reporting systems. High initial costs often delay sustainability investments despite their long-term benefits.
Environmental management practices also vary across the sector. While leading factories use advanced wastewater treatment and chemical management systems, many production clusters still face challenges in textile waste management and circular economy adoption.
Labour-related challenges also remain, including wages, worker representation, skills development, and human rights due diligence. Manufacturers must also navigate complex buyer requirements, certification schemes, and regulatory frameworks, which can increase audit fatigue and compliance costs.
To remain globally competitive, Bangladesh’s RMG sector must move beyond compliance-driven sustainability and establish sustainability as a core business strategy.
This requires stronger governance, improved reporting systems, and integration of ESG priorities into corporate decision-making, risk management, and investment planning.
Wider adoption of global reporting frameworks, independent assurance mechanisms, and digital traceability solutions will be essential to improve transparency, credibility, and data quality across the value chain.
At the same time, an inclusive sustainability transition will require targeted support for SMEs through technical assistance, capacity building, and access to affordable green finance.
Collaboration among manufacturers, global brands, policy-makers, financial institutions, development partners, and academic institutions will be critical to overcome barriers and accelerate industry-wide transformation.
Bangladesh’s RMG industry has demonstrated its ability to adapt by improving workplace safety, strengthening compliance systems, and advancing sustainable factory practices.
However, the next stage of competitiveness will depend on transforming sustainability from a set of operational initiatives into a measurable and strategic advantage.
As global apparel sourcing increasingly prioritizes carbon performance, resource efficiency, transparency, human rights, and accountability, cost competitiveness alone will no longer be sufficient.
The central challenge now for Bangladesh is to institutionalize credible sustainability reporting and ensure that responsible practices are embedded throughout the industry.
By doing so, Bangladesh can strengthen buyer confidence, secure long-term market access, and maintain its position as a global apparel leader.
Mohammad Rabiul Kabir is an associate professor at Stamford University, Bangladesh, and a sustainability and ESG professional.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with France. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
At a time when the Bangladesh economy is experiencing a particularly challenging period, it is more important than ever to strengthen our diplomatic relations with nations.
To that end, the visit of the French Senate delegation and their expressed interest in deeper political engagement with Bangladesh is an important moment, and one that Dhaka should seize with clarity and ambition.
France, beyond being a major European power, is also a strategic actor in global security, climate diplomacy, and development cooperation. Strengthening ties with Paris serves Bangladesh’s long‑term interests, especially as we navigate our economic and social challenges in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.
The senators’ remarks signal that France sees Bangladesh as more than a development partner and views it as a country with growing regional influence and a role to play in Indo‑Pacific dynamics.
This recognition matters and opens the door to more robust cooperation in areas where France has deep expertise: defense modernization, renewable energy, climate expertise, digital governance, and higher education.
Bangladesh, for its part, has every reason to welcome this interest. France has been a consistent supporter of Bangladesh, be it the climate agenda, infrastructure development, or being a growing market for Bangladeshi goods.
With Bangladesh eventually needing to shed its LDC tag, stronger political engagement with France can help diversify partnerships, expand trade opportunities, and strengthen diplomatic leverage in the entirety of Europe.
Bangladesh, for its part, must articulate clear priorities, from technology transfer and green energy investment to cultural exchanges. Engagement must also move beyond courtesy visits and translate into structured dialogue, joint initiatives, and long‑term agreements.
Bangladesh has the opportunity to deepen a relationship built on mutual respect and shared global concerns with a major European nation. We must not squander it. Stronger ties with Paris will not only enhance Bangladesh’s international standing but also support its aspirations for sustainable development, climate resilience, and eventually, a more prosperous future.

item.title: The non-residential Bangladeshi: Reform or ruin?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is an old, unwritten law: You can take a Bangladeshi out of the country, but you can rarely extract the country from the Bangladeshi.
When a person steps off a flight at Heathrow or JFK, a silent internal split occurs.
The passport changes, the currency in the wallet shifts, but the underlying psychological software -- that intricate, centuries-old wiring shaped by deltaic floods, agrarian survivalism, and localized territoriality -- remains intact.
This raises an uncomfortable, introspective question: Does life abroad genuinely elevate the non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) psyche, or does it merely provide a grander, more lucrative stage for domestic vices?
There is a comforting, widely peddled myth popular in living rooms across Dhaka and Chittagong: That the average Bangladeshi, notoriously prone to skipping queues and bribing their way out of trouble back home, magically transforms into a law-abiding saint the moment they step foot into a Western nation.
The argument usually points to the omnipresent "rule of law" -- the strict speed cameras, the unbribable police, the automated tax audits, and the certainty of punishment.
In Bangladesh, institutional fragility turns law into an optional menu of suggestions; abroad, it is assumed, the sheer weight of enforcement forces instant moral reform.
Yet, public record reveals a far more complicated psychological reality. The rule of law certainly creates external compliance, but it does not automatically erase decades of ingrained survival instincts.
For a significant cohort, the presence of a structured, trusting system does not inspire civic duty -- it merely changes the nature of the game.
Where law back home is evaded through brute influence or financial bribes, abroad it is often tested through administrative loophole-hunting, calculated anonymity, and systemic arbitrage.
To trace the psychological shifts of the diaspora, one must look at the historical trail left in the press and legal archives.
The migration waves of the 1980s and 1990s -- particularly to the United Kingdom and Southern Europe -- brought not just workforce muscle, but also the instinctual survival mechanisms of the homeland.
In the late 1980s and through the 1990s, British media periodically highlighted complex welfare and housing benefit scams originating out of East London’s Tower Hamlets -- a hub heavily settled by Sylheti families.
What local authorities framed as sophisticated "social security fraud" was often, at its core, the psychological extension of shonchoy (survival hoarding) and system-gaming honed in a home country where state institutions were meant to be bypassed, not trusted.
By the mid-2010s, investigative operations in Europe laid bare even stranger phenomena: Operations where Bangladeshi migrants holding Italian passports were flying into London on day trips to lodge fraudulent welfare claims before flying back out.
In Australia, immigration reports over the decades have quietly documented cash-in-hand wage undercutting, pseudo-marriages for permanent residency, and localized rental "hot-bedding" schemes run by established diaspora landlords exploiting newly arrived countrymen.
To the foreign observer, these act as felonies or administrative crimes.
But to an introspective Bangladeshi, they are recognizable reflexes.
The rule of law deters blatant chaos, but it cannot prevent the scarcity-driven impulse to extract maximum resources with minimal exposure.
When we look into the mirror, we see ancestral traits that refused to dissolve in foreign waters.
Take the stereotypical Noakhali ethos: Fiercely hardworking, notoriously tight-knit, possessing an innate commercial shrewdness, and an uncompromising loyalty to the clan.
When transported to London’s Brick Lane, New York’s Jackson Heights, or Sydney’s Lakemba, this trait morphs into an enclave mentality.
It creates vibrant business ecosystems, but it can also create isolated echo chambers where Western civil code is treated as an external inconvenience, and the primary moral obligation remains owed strictly to one's immediate lineage back home.
Conversely, consider the Barisal archetype: Deeply opinionated, intellectually pugnacious, and harbouring an ingrained skepticism toward formal authority -- a product of living in a riverine landscape where land itself shifts overnight.
Overseas, this manifests as a refusal to quietly assimilate.
It can express itself as political factionalism -- where Bangladeshi political rivalries are absurdly re-enacted in municipal hall meetings -- or as an instinctive urge to find the hidden loophole in any structured bureaucracy.
Yet, to characterize the NRB experience solely through its missteps is to miss a profound psychological evolution.
Migration is a pressure cooker. While the weak points of the psyche can rupture into criminality under stress, its strengths -- when paired with actual rule of law -- can crystallize into extraordinary global achievement.
For those who genuinely allow the structural stability of foreign nations to alter their internal compass, the transformation is real:
For these individuals, living abroad broke the chain of scarcity mindsets.
It replaced the anxiety of bluffing through life with genuine mastery, allowing the inherent warmth, hospitality, and intelligence of the Bangladeshi character to shine through without the corrupting friction of institutional decay.
Does the non-resident Bangladeshi change for the better or the worse? The truth is that migration acts as a magnifier, not an automatic moral cleanser.
The presence of the rule of law creates a fork in the road rather than a guaranteed transformation.
If a person departs Bangladesh viewing rules merely as obstacles to dodge, foreign soil simply provides a more stable, lucrative infrastructure to game.
The bad gets worse because the safety nets of wealthy nations offer higher stakes to exploit.
However, if a person uses the predictability of foreign law to shed the hyper-vigilance required to survive back home, the Bangladeshi psyche undergoes a remarkable transformation.
The raw energy used for survival converts into an unmatched work ethic. The clannish loyalty expands into genuine civic responsibility.
The NRB remains forever caught between two worlds: Carrying the river's chaos in their blood, while deciding whether to respect or exploit the paved, orderly streets of the world.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Getting serious about dengue prevention. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s inauguration of the three‑month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign is a reminder once again that Bangladesh cannot afford complacency when it comes to the disease.
Dengue continues to claim lives while hospitals remain strained, and the next three months are considered the highest‑risk period. The PM’s message is clear and one that ought to have been heeded years ago: Dengue cannot be controlled by mosquito‑killing drives alone; it requires public awareness, daily vigilance, and collective responsibility.
The campaign’s emphasis on keeping surroundings clean and removing stagnant water every day reflects the core truth of dengue prevention. Aedes mosquitoes breed in small, overlooked pockets of water -- flowerpots, rooftop corners, discarded containers, construction sites, and household drains.
No city corporation, no ministry, and no volunteer force can eliminate these breeding grounds without active participation from residents.
The PM’s call for coordinated field‑level activities involving local administrations, volunteers, students, and community groups recognizes that dengue prevention must be woven into everyday life.
Around 25,000 volunteers have reportedly already joined the campaign, and this sort of intent shown is the kind of energy we need to turn this campaign into a success.
Yet, while weekly visits to homes and establishments will help identify breeding sites and raise awareness, their efforts will only succeed if households respond -- by cleaning regularly, checking rooftops and balconies, clearing drains, and refusing to let water accumulate.
The PM’s directive to intensify awareness campaigns across television, mass media, and social media underscores the urgency of changing public behaviour, not just public policy.
We have continued to struggle with dengue because prevention has often been reactive, triggered only after outbreaks worsen. This campaign must mark a shift toward proactive, sustained action.
Dengue is preventable. Bangladesh must prove that it can prevent it.

item.title: The succession question returns to haunt Awami League. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A name has suddenly surfaced across Bangladeshi social media and various established media outlets, a name well known in political circles but one that had not been mentioned publicly for quite some time.
Sheikh Fazlul Karim Selim has not only returned to the spotlight, but his name has also sparked a genuine debate both within and outside his party.
This debate was initiated by Sheikh Hasina herself.
In a telephonic interview with the Indian online news portal The Wall, Hasina remarked that Sheikh Selim could assume responsibility for the party in her absence.
Although she described this as a temporary measure in accordance with the party’s constitution, many interpreted it as a sign that she had chosen Sheikh Selim as her successor.
This assumption gave rise to various speculations, such as the idea that Sheikh Hasina was stepping away from politics or retiring, or that she had realized a return to Dhaka was no longer possible and was therefore handing over responsibility to Sheikh Selim.
The actual context, however, was different.
Amal Sarkar, executive editor of The Wall, had raised the issue during the interview. He asked who would take charge of the party if Sheikh Hasina were to be imprisoned or taken into custody by an agency for interrogation upon her return to Dhaka.
In response, Sheikh Hasina explained the Awami League’s constitution, stating that the most senior member of the Presidium would assume responsibility in such a scenario.
Currently, of the 16 Presidium members, three have passed away, six are in prison, one’s whereabouts are unknown, and six remain active. Among them, Sheikh Selim is the most senior.
The explanation is clear. A similar situation arose during the 2007-08 “1/11” government era when Sheikh Hasina was imprisoned.
At the time, senior Presidium member Zillur Rahman took charge. That did not mean he had been designated as Hasina’s successor to the party presidency.
While the matter appears straightforward, there is no doubt that the mention of Sheikh Selim’s name fuelled the subsequent rumours and speculation.
Sheikh Selim has been elected to the National Parliament nine times. This fact alone sends a clear message about his popularity and local influence in Gopalganj.
He is the nephew of Bangladesh’s founding leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, specifically, Sheikh Hasina’s paternal cousin.
Perhaps because of this close familial relationship, many view Sheikh Selim not merely as someone who could take “temporary charge,” but as a potential permanent successor. That is precisely where the complication lies.
A Dhaka-based news portal has already reported that several senior leaders currently in Kolkata held a meeting and expressed disagreement with Hasina’s decision.
The report further stated that they proposed Jahangir Kabir Nanak for the role.
The issue here is that some observers have questioned the credibility of the report, even raising doubts about whether such a meeting actually took place.
Regardless, one thing is clear: There is no unanimous support for Sheikh Selim among Awami League leaders and activists.
Many perceive him as the kind of leader who “disappears during times of crisis.” And this is not merely about Sheikh Selim; the episode signals a deepening crisis within the Awami League.
The reported meeting is merely an indication of how acute the infighting among the party’s leaders in exile has become.
Ever since Sheikh Hasina’s tenure began, this question has been raised repeatedly, yet no satisfactory answer has ever emerged.
Who comes after Sheikh Hasina? Who will take the helm of the Awami League if Hasina retires? Does she have any plans regarding succession?
There has never been a direct answer to these questions.
Whenever confronted with this question, Hasina would say that the party would decide who its leader should be.
However, no one considered the possibility that the party might not be in a position to make such a decision when the time came.
By closing off the path to a transfer of power through elections, the Awami League perhaps believed it could safely remain in power for the long haul.
Yet, having enjoyed the comforts of governance for so long, the party, once a force that shook the streets, forgot that there are far more perilous paths to a change of power than elections.
It was precisely through such a perilous path that it was forced to relinquish power in 2024.
Since the fall of the Awami League, the question has resurfaced: Is a change in leadership on the horizon? How exactly will it happen, and who will step in?
Various people have attempted to answer these questions in different ways.
Many had assumed that the Awami League would be restructured around members against whom there were no allegations of serious crimes.
However, it became evident that even if a leader faced no such accusations at the time, the very moment they began the task of reorganizing the party, their name could be implicated in a case involving murder or “crimes against humanity.”
Yet, talk began circulating about a so-called “refined” or “reformed” Awami League. Names such as Saber Hossain Chowdhury, Shirin Sharmin Chaudhury, and even Narayanganj Mayor Selina Hayat Ivy were linked to this idea, although none of them publicly spoke of playing a role in restructuring the party.
However, one thing became clear: Regardless of the extent to which former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina bears responsibility for the Awami League’s current plight, in the eyes of the party’s grassroots activists, there is no leader other than her.
If the party were to be restructured under someone else’s leadership, it might remain a political party, but it would certainly cease to be the Awami League as they know it.
On the other hand, conversations with Awami League members, including former members of Parliament, over the past year or so suggest that if Sheikh Hasina herself were to initiate a transition process and select a successor, the rank and file might well accept that new leadership.
Yet there is another complication.
Over the last five decades, Bangladesh’s two major parties, the Awami League and the BNP, have become excessively dependent on particular families.
The BNP has never managed to step out of the shadow of its founder, Ziaur Rahman, nor has it made any serious attempt to do so.
The party is well aware that without the umbrella of the Zia family, its unity could crumble.
To keep the party together, leadership passed from General Zia to his wife, Khaleda Zia, and subsequently to their son, Tarique Rahman.
The situation within the Awami League is somewhat different.
Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was not the party’s founder; the Awami League was established by Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani and Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy.
However, under Sheikh Mujib’s leadership, the Awami League became the embodiment of the hopes and aspirations of the Bengali people in what was then East Pakistan.
It was under Sheikh Mujib that the party spearheaded the movement for self-determination and contested the 1970 elections. He provided the direction for the independence movement in March 1971, and the subsequent Liberation War was fought in his name.
Because of this historical continuity, and the fact that Mujib and almost his entire family were killed on August 15, 1975, the Awami League became inextricably linked with the Sheikh family.
Despite the presence of prominent leaders within the party following Mujib’s assassination, they brought Sheikh Hasina back from exile in 1981 to take the helm.
It would come as no surprise if, during these difficult times for the Awami League, party leaders and activists once again looked towards the Sheikh family.
A parallel can be drawn with the BNP, where party members naturally accepted Khaleda Zia’s son, Tarique Rahman, as her successor.
Whether it is a matter of temporary responsibility or long-term succession, there is no doubt that the Awami League must contemplate its post-Hasina future.
At the same time, however, it must address how to regain public trust following 2024.
There appear to be two clear reasons for the party’s current organizational stagnation and crisis of morale.
First is the issue of leadership. Despite the continued faith in Sheikh Hasina, the Awami League is currently, effectively, leaderless.
Whether because of the ban on its activities, the imprisonment or flight abroad of many leaders, or the looming threat of legal cases hanging over many, the bottom line is that the party faces an acute leadership crisis.
Second, the Awami League has failed to come to terms with the events of 2024, even after two years. There appears to have been no internal self-criticism or even a meaningful process of introspection within the party.
Its leaders remain fixated on conspiracy theories and continue to deny their own culpability.
The Awami League needs to ask itself some critical questions:
Why did the movement to oust the government occur?
Why did a movement become necessary to bring about a change in government?
Why did students repeatedly take to the streets?
Why did the urban middle class support the movement?
Why did so many people lose their lives?
The answers to these questions will determine the message the party conveys to the public.
If the Awami League views itself as a party of the people, it must be accountable to them.
It is through this process of accountability that the party’s future leadership may become clear.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster.

item.title: Antimicrobial resistance: The silent pandemic. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Most of us think infections come from outside invaders; harmful germs that enter the body and make us sick.
However, some microbes of growing concern are not strangers; they are long-term residents of our own bodies.
The human body is like a busy neighbourhood, home to trillions of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses.
Together, they form what scientists call the microbiome. Most of these tiny residents are not enemies. They help digest food, strengthen the immune system, and protect us from harmful germs.
For the most part, we live peacefully with these microbes. But when this delicate balance is disturbed, some of our friendly neighbours can become opportunistic pathogens.
In the age of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), these once-manageable microbes are becoming increasingly difficult to control.
Take Escherichia coli ( E coli ), for example. It normally lives in our intestines and plays an important role in maintaining gut health. But if it enters the urinary tract, it can cause infection.
Until recently, these infections were usually easy to treat. Today, many E coli strains no longer respond to commonly used antibiotics.
According to a landmark study published in The Lancet in 2022, six leading pathogens collectively accounted for nearly 1 million AMR-attributable deaths in 2019, with E coli being the single largest individual contributor.
The same is true for Candida , a fungus that normally lives quietly in our mouths and digestive system. Most of the time, it causes no harm. But when the immune system is weakened by illness, cancer treatment, or prolonged antibiotic use, it can multiply rapidly and cause serious, sometimes life-threatening, infections.
Another example is Staphylococcus aureus , a bacterium commonly found on our skin and inside the nose. Many people carry it without ever becoming ill.
However, some strains have evolved resistance to important antibiotics, making infections much more difficult and costly to treat.
One of the biggest reasons is the misuse and overuse of antibiotics. Every time antibiotics are taken unnecessarily, used incorrectly, or stopped too early, bacteria are given another opportunity to adapt.
Over time, they develop ways to survive medicines that once killed them.
In a sense, we are unintentionally training our microscopic neighbours to defend themselves.
This is no longer just a concern for scientists and doctors; it is a growing global public health problem.
In Bangladesh, this problem is easy to observe in everyday life. A parent may visit a local pharmacy for a child with a fever or a common cold and receive an antibiotic without a prescription, even though many of these illnesses are caused by viruses, against which antibiotics do not work.
While this may seem like a quick solution, repeated unnecessary use encourages bacteria to become resistant.
Studies have shown that antibiotics are frequently purchased without a prescription in Bangladesh, highlighting the urgent need for stronger antibiotic stewardship and greater public awareness.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the misuse and overuse of antibiotics are among the leading drivers of antimicrobial resistance worldwide.
Resistant infections lead to longer hospital stays, higher healthcare costs, and fewer treatment options. They also threaten many of the medical advances we now take for granted.
Safe surgery, cancer treatment, intensive care, and the care of newborn babies all depend on antibiotics that work.
The answer is not to eliminate the microbes that live with us. Most are essential for our health.
Instead, we must preserve the delicate balance between humans and the microorganisms that share our bodies.
That requires responsible antibiotic use, stronger infection prevention, better public awareness, and effective antimicrobial stewardship programs.
Healthcare professionals, policy-makers, pharmacists, and the public all have important roles to play.
Antimicrobial resistance is often called a silent pandemic because it spreads quietly, without the dramatic headlines of outbreaks like Covid-19. Yet its impact could be just as devastating.
The World Health Organization has identified AMR as one of the top 10 global public health threats facing humanity. The microbes that have lived alongside us need not become our enemies. Whether they remain trusted neighbours or dangerous adversaries will depend largely on the choices we make today.
ASM Tarik Hasan is a public health researcher specializing in antimicrobial resistance and clinical microbiology.

item.title: The quiet strain of working mothers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every working mother in Bangladesh endures an exhausting dual existence. In one scenario, you're juggling the pressures of a typical 9-to-5 job -- attending back-to-back meetings, receiving urgent client calls, meeting tight deadlines, and striving for career goals.
In the other world, your mind remains permanently tethered to a phone sitting next to your keyboard, quietly waiting for updates from home.
Has my baby eaten? Did he take his bath? Is he crying?
As a new mother of a seven-month-old boy, I never imagined how challenging it would be to cross this mental difference.
Motherhood is meant to be a journey of connection, yet every morning feels like a quiet tug-of-war.
Like any mother, I wish I could experience every fleeting moment of his early months without blinking.
Yet, my hands are tied. Every morning, I pack my bags, say goodbye, and leave my son in the care of my ageing mother before stepping into the office.
While I am really lucky to have family support, this arrangement has replaced one type of anxiety with another.
Throughout my workday, a constant loop of fear runs in the background: Did my mother remember to take her medicine while keeping up with an energetic infant? What if something terrible happens while I am locked in a presentation -- how will she manage alone?
This constant tension is not unique to my household; it reflects the daily reality of hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of urban working women across Bangladesh.
Relying on grandparents is a temporary patch, not a sustainable solution -- it places heavy physical strain on elderly parents while leaving working mothers carrying an inescapable sense of guilt.
The true tragedy is that this strain arrives at the worst possible moment in a woman's career.
Most of us spend 25 or 26 years pursuing higher education and building professional foundations. Yet, just as female professionals reach their prime years for career advancement, the arrival of a child creates a stark ultimatum.
Without accessible, institutional childcare, a vast number of women are forced to step away from the workforce at the precise moment they are ready to step into leadership.
This mid-career exit represents a massive, preventable leak in our country's talent pipeline.
Section 94 of the Bangladesh Labour Act mandates that every establishment employing 40 or more women must maintain a suitable room for children under the age of six.
Yet across corporations, institutions, and factories, compliance remains largely symbolic or entirely absent.
Where daycare facilities do exist, capacity rarely meets demand.
Childcare should not be treated as a woman's personal dilemma or a luxury corporate perk. When workplaces integrate safe, professionally managed, and on-site daycare facilities, childcare ceases to be an overwhelming burden borne by one person at home.
It creates an ecosystem where fathers can also take active, equal roles in daily caregiving during work hours.
If Bangladesh aims to sustain its economic growth and empower its female workforce, care infrastructure must be prioritized as essential national infrastructure. Until employers and policy-makers build safe harbours for our children where we work, our brightest women will continue to be forced out of the workforce -- not for a lack of ambition, but for a lack of support.
Jerin Tasnim is a senior executive, HR, Dhaka Tribune and Bangla Tribune.

item.title: They looted the banks. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We've got to get this firmly in our minds that they looted the banks. As this newspaper reports : “Nearly Tk33 of every Tk100 lent by banks is now in default.”
Now, some of this is just banking. There're always some loans that go bad. People borrowed and things didn't work out. The amount of interest charged on loans reflects this, the knowledge that some will not be repaid.
So, every loan has to pay 1%, or 2%, more, to cover the 2 or 3% of loans that don't get repaid. It's just part of the business.
But one third of loans going bad? That's either the effect of a dreadful recession -- depression -- or evidence of looting. Bangladesh hasn't had a recent depression, therefore our conclusion should be that, well, you can add in the rest.
As to who “they” were or are, we can all have a good guess. But we'll not mention specific names, obviously, since libel laws do exist.
But, well, people with good and close connections with the previous political regime would be a good guide.
As to why they looted the banks, that's easier, as Willy Sutton said. He was a US bank robber and when asked why he stole from banks said: “That's where the money is.”
And if you've got political power, it's a lot easier to steal from the banks than it is from the government.
Certainly, the government spends a lot of money, but stealing tax money is still difficult. But banks exist to make loans. So, if you've political power, then you can force -- or even just “persuade” -- the banks to lend you money which you've no intention of repaying.
This does become a loss of tax money eventually, as we're finding out. Because the government that comes afterwards has to do something about those banks and those loans.
Which is what is being done and is what has to be done. As the banks have been looted, we have two, and only two, choices.
We'll stop depositing our money in banks -- as has been happening -- and that means we'll all be poorer in the future. Because what banks do, as an economic factor, is repurpose our savings into the investments that make the future richer. If we all stop using banks for our savings this will not happen.
We also have to prosecute those who took the money. Bankrupt them for not repaying. Take their businesses off them. A few in jail would be a very good idea indeed.
We also need to make sure that the political system does not determine such lending again in the future. There's no point in getting rid of one bunch of thieves just to allow another to repeat the exercise.
But one more thing. Some of those loans were just looting. But many of them -- even most of them -- were for at least attempts at investing.
We all recall the minister who tried to build an international property portfolio, right? Who bought at the peak and has been seeing the value of the properties falling since he bought?
That's the thing to really remember from this. Those in politics, or even those closely allied with politics, do not in fact know what to do with the money.
They cannot even invest free money profitably. Therefore, the new system should not only insist upon no looting but also no investing by politics, politicians, and the politically associated.
Thieves are always with us, and it's a very good idea not to give them access to our money. But politicians, the politically aligned, are also -- even if honest -- terribly bad investors. So we should also not give them access to our money.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Do not repeat the same mistakes with cybersecurity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh’s concerns about the draft Cyber Security (Amendment) Act, 2026 deserve serious attention.
As written, the proposed law risks repeating the mistakes of previous regimes -- vague language, unchecked authority, and broad surveillance powers had been a mainstay with previous cybersecurity laws.
There is no questioning the fact that such laws were used to silence dissent rather than protect citizens. Bangladesh cannot afford to walk that path again.
As rightfully noted by TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman: “The draft law brings three complex and distinct issues -- cybercrime, cybersecurity and people’s right to freedom of expression -- under a single law, without giving adequate attention to any of them."
Deliberate misinterpretation and misuse of our cyber laws have been weapons for the previous administration, violating the human rights of many. We must move away from vagueness in our laws that create a landscape where interpretation becomes discretionary, enforcement becomes arbitrary, and ultimately citizens become vulnerable.
When terms such as “rumour,” “misinformation,” “demeaning,” “defamatory,” and “insulting to the state” are defined loosely, authorities have the power to target criticism, satire, or legitimate political speech. Our history suggests that such ambiguities have repeatedly been weaponized by the state at the expense of the people.
Equally troubling is the proposal for a 28-member Cyber Security Council dominated by government representatives. A council structured this way risks becoming an enforcement arm rather than an independent oversight body.
No good comes from sweeping powers without accountability, combined with immunity for actions taken in “good faith.” All they usually achieve is undermining the principle that all are equal before the law.
We are not arguing that Bangladesh’s digital space must be protected from cybercrime and genuine threats, which is a given. But protection cannot come at the cost of fundamental rights.
Laws that blur definitions, expand surveillance, and criminalize expression do not strengthen cybersecurity but weaken democracy. Our digital future must be secure, but it must also be free. This is what the present administration must ensure.

item.title: Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Where do Muslim youths fit in India's 'Cockroach' protests?

Submitted by Nabiya Khan on Fri, 09/04/2026 - 20:06
The country harbours a political culture where exercising the right to demonstrate is safer for some than for others
A CJP supporter waves the national flag a day after the resignation of India’s education minister, in Mumbai on 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjpe/AFP)
Off

As protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi gained momentum this summer, many Muslims urged their children not to participate. 

Some mosque announcements cautioned Muslim youths to stay away - not over any clash with the movement’s ideals, but amid fears of harassment, false charges, hounding and intimidation.

For many students, attending protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar was a way to show they cared enough about the issues facing the country to show up. But Muslim students in today’s India must always weigh the consequences of their actions. 

Other Muslim student activists have spent years languishing in jail, without trial and with little hope of bail. Some have had their homes demolished. 

In the eyes of the government, Muslim comes first, and student later. Staying home might look like political apathy from the outside, but inside the community, it is a safety valve, underscoring the limits of what Muslims in India can afford to do.

For a generation of young Indians, the CJP has made it easier to imagine themselves as political actors. The movement - which started out as a joke after appalling remarks by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who compared unemployed youths to “cockroaches” - quickly moved from social media to the streets. 

As the protests spread nationwide, they attracted large numbers of young people angry about exam failures, unemployment, and the absence of accountability in a system upon which their futures depend. Thousands marched towards parliament, and on 25 July, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Political exposure

The warnings to Muslim youths, cautioning them against participation in this countrywide movement, did not stem only from fear. They came from a community with years of experience as to what political exposure can mean. 

Protests over the Citizenship Amendment Act, a law that excludes Muslim immigrants and refugees living in India from obtaining citizenship, are part of this same historical memory. The ensuing crackdown culminated in February 2020, when state-orchestrated communal violence in northeastern Delhi killed 53 people, most of them Muslims. 

The violence was followed by arrests under anti-terrorism legislation, with some of those arrested still in jail years later without trial.

For communities that have repeatedly experienced police targeting, surveillance and violence after political mobilisation, caution is based on experience. Despite such fears, some Muslims still participated in the CJP protests; among them was Mohammad Junaid, who alleges that he was subsequently harassed by police. 

You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem

The CJP movement has made a point of saying that its politics belong to young Indians. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has repeatedly argued that Indian politics has spent too long on Hindu-vs-Muslim issues, and that education and employment should take precedence. 

There is a reasonable political frustration behind this argument. A student whose exam has been cancelled should not have to choose a religion before demanding justice. 

For Muslims, however, communal politics is not a subject that can simply be put aside so that everyone can get back to talking about education and jobs. It follows them into those areas. It affects how they are spoken about, how their neighbourhoods are policed, and how their political actions are read.

The history behind this is longer than Prime Minister Narendra Modi or the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Author Vinayak Damodar Savarkar set out the ideological foundations of Hindutva in his 1923 work Essentials of Hindutva, defining the nation through an idea of Hindu cultural belonging that placed Muslims and Christians outside the same conception of national identity. 

Modi’s years in power have merely brought an old majoritarian politics deeper into the institutions and everyday life of the country. 

Language of incitement

There have been vigilante attacks on Muslims, unlawful demolitions of Muslim homes and businesses, and the expulsion of Bengali-speaking Muslims and Rohingya refugees to Bangladesh. Modi himself made Muslims a central target of his 2024 campaign. 

This is the environment in which a Muslim student decides whether a protest is worth attending.

At the same time, the language of incitement coming from the government has continuously shifted. Modi recently revived the term “dimagi Naxal” to refer to an intellectual insurgency, and the BJP quickly turned the phrase into a coordinated meme campaign on social media, targeting CJP protesters, among others. 

Muslims know this language well. They have been called infiltrators, terrorists and anti-national long before the introduction of “dimagi Naxal”. This does not necessarily mean that every Hindu sees Muslims as a threat, but it does mean that political parties can build an electoral advantage by making Muslims the group against which the majority is asked to measure its own safety and interests. 

For Indian Muslims the end times have arrived
Read More »

In a country where the BJP has won a third consecutive national term by pushing a project based on the systemic extermination of Muslims, these politics cannot be treated as background noise.

That is why blanket statements about “fighting for Indian youth” - while avoiding the word “Muslim”, or refusing to discuss Muslim political prisoners - creates a problem. The CJP can decide not to make Muslims its organising constituency, but it cannot assume that refusing to name Muslims makes communal politics less real.

The success of the CJP thus leaves India with a problem larger than exam leaks. The movement showed that young people can organise, sustain pressure, and make a government act. 

A democracy cannot measure the health of its protest culture only by the number of people who turn up. It has to ask who can turn up without calculating how their surname, neighbourhood or religion might affect them after the protests.

The BJP has made communal politics part of everyday life in India. Muslims have lived with its consequences for years: being called infiltrators and security threats, as their neighbourhoods, homes and activities come under increasing scrutiny. 

These are not side issues. You cannot claim to fight the disease, while telling people living with its symptoms that their suffering is a distraction from the real problem. 

A country can have a constitutional right to protest, while still harbouring a political culture where exercising that right is safer for some than for others. That gap is where democracy is tested. India’s young Muslims know this already. The CJP movement should learn it before it can honestly speak for all.

item.title: Developing nations must work together. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With September 12 marking the UN Day for South-South Cooperation, Bangladesh must recognize the importance of cooperation among developing countries and actively work to strengthen its ties.
Indeed, it would not be a mistake to argue that most meaningful development partnerships increasingly lie within the Global South.
This day reflects a shift in global power, knowledge, and innovation. Developing nations now generate a substantial share of global growth, and their collective experience offers solutions far more relevant to our realities than traditional models originating in the developed North.
Bangladesh has repeatedly benefited from exchanges with fellow developing nations, be they agricultural techniques, disaster‑management expertise, digital‑governance models, renewable‑energy solutions, or public health innovations.
It goes without saying that solutions have greater odds of success when there is an exchange of context‑appropriate tools shaped by countries that have confronted similar constraints and pressures.
It must also be stated that Bangladesh is not merely a recipient, and its achievements in community‑based health systems, microfinance, disaster preparedness, and social‑protection programs have become global references for other nations in the Global South.
South-South cooperation allows Bangladesh to share these strengths while gaining new approaches to emerging challenges such as climate shocks, rapid urbanization, food insecurity, and digital transformation.
Given the importance, it is imperative that we deepen this engagement. Too often, cooperation remains limited to conferences, pilot projects, or symbolic agreements.
Bangladesh needs long‑term partnerships, ones that expand joint research, strengthen climate resilience, and reduce dependence on external models that do not align with our local realities.
The Global South’s collective future depends on how effectively its members learn from one another and build systems rooted in solidarity rather than hierarchy.
This cooperation could be a central pillar of a fairer, more resilient future for all of us.

item.title: Protecting the hand that hurts. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Picture a courtroom in Bangladesh. A woman is sitting on a bench, hiding her bruises, and waiting to testify against her own husband who beats her mercilessly.
When her name is called, she suddenly changes her original story, fervently trying to withdraw the case and convince the magistrate that her injuries were rather the result of an accident.
Outside the courtroom, her mother-in-law is standing, waiting for her to take her to the same house, the same husband, and the same violence.
This is not a rare scenario in Bangladesh’s family courts or police stations; rather, it is a pattern so common here that oftentimes the police or the court shows reluctance to even register cases of domestic violence.
Why do these women, despite years of abuse, try to protect their abusers?
To answer this question, let us travel 53 years into the past.
In 1973, four employees (three women and one man) of Kreditbanken Bank in Stockholm were taken hostage by two robbers for six days.
By the time the police were able to free them, they had grown protective of their captors, refusing to testify against the perpetrators and instead raising money for their legal defense.
Psychiatrists called this condition Stockholm Syndrome; a survival response where the victim develops sympathy, even loyalty toward the abuser who controls their fear.
Similarly, among women who are victims of abuse, a long period of intimate violence and torture produces Stockholm Syndrome in the form of fierce trauma bonding, which leads to an unintentional instinct to protect their abuser from consequences of their own.
In Bangladesh’s household scenario, this trauma bond rarely announces itself as a pathology; rather, it looks like a housewife telling her neighbours that the bruises on her face are from an accidental fall down the stairs, a mother telling her daughter to call the injuries on her body marks of a self-inflicted accident, or a young wife defending her husband’s violence as occasional outbursts of anger.
According to analysts, the main reasons for South Asian women experiencing Stockholm Syndrome are financial dependency, fear of social stigma, patriarchal society, and a conviction that suffering silently is a form of loyalty and a badge of honour for women. A woman's own family often supports this idea of protecting the abusive husband at any cost.
This is akin to the boiling-frog pattern, where researchers illustrate that when abuse towards a woman increases gradually, she can lose the ability or the willingness to protect herself or remove herself from the situation.
Based on the irrational belief that the world cannot offer her a better alternative than what she already has, she thus ends up subconsciously developing instincts to protect her abusive partner.
To make things worse, the Domestic Violence Act (2010) in Bangladesh every so often clashes head-on with the involuntary, deep state of self-preservation in women who have been conditioned to defend their abusers.
As a result, police, often reluctantly, send complaints back for domestic violence matters to be settled “domestically.”
Millions of women enable their partners to continue abusing them throughout their relationships. However, putting the onus of standing up to violence on the victims themselves is easy but, by no means, fair.
Instead, we need to ask the difficult questions here.
Why, after all, do the abused women enable their abusers? And why do they keep protecting these sadist oppressors?
A quick glance at these ill-fated women’s formative years will tell you why.
Since their early days, many women see their mothers silently suffer physical and mental torture, verbal assault, and various other forms of hostility in their own house.
These women keep hearing from their family, neighbours, relatives, and everyone else in society that domestic disputes are normal between married couples, that “purush manush ektu emoni hoy, meye der manay nite hoy” (men will be men and women need to adjust), that a woman’s real house is her husband’s house, and that a good wife should prioritize her family honour and endure her husband’s maltreatment at any cost.
The mass media these women become exposed to during the developmental period further normalizes and even glamorizes violence against women.
Many movies, dramas, and even cartoons typically characterize women as damsels in distress and men as their saviors, romanticizing toxic relationships and portraying physical violence as a sign of passionate love.
Essentially, when a woman is repetitively told that she is a nobody without her husband, the narrative gets fixated in her mind.
Sometimes this narrative can become so noxious that women even end up becoming complicit in their husbands’ crimes. In the brutal Ramisa rape and murder case, for instance, the wife of the offender actively took part in the atrocity.
While this woman’s crimes are unforgivable, have we ever stopped to think that perhaps it was Stockholm Syndrome that made her feel compelled to protect her husband?
What can be done to save these women from themselves? Do we really believe that only enforcing stricter laws against domestic violence, getting more women educated, or helping women become financially independent will solve the issue?
Admittedly, a combined effort from all these fronts will likely improve the situation to a certain extent. However, until and unless our society recalibrates its views on domestic violence and stops telling women to adjust, accept, and adapt, women will continue to protect the very hand that hurts them.
Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at BRAC Business School and Faizah Zahin is an English and Humanities student, BRAC University.

item.title: On the road again. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
My sister and her retired husband have benefited from forms of support that would be unimaginable in many countries. Assistance with household tasks, social support, and allied health services can help older people and people with disabilities remain at home and maintain a degree of independence.
Australia's aged-care system formally includes services such as social work and physiotherapy among the forms of support that can be provided in home and community settings.
Australia's relatively high wages are another part of this social model. As of July 2026, the national minimum wage is A$26.44 an hour, or A$1,004.90 for a 38-hour week,
Singapore provides another fascinating example.
I spent a couple of weeks there and was struck by what highly educated, pragmatic, and institutionally minded leadership can accomplish when it is combined with administrative competence and a long-term vision.
I visited a school whose principal had become something of a legendary figure. He had grown up poor and had been supported by teachers from religious communities different from his own. His life story was therefore a personal testament to the possibilities of education and merit.
He also played an important role in promoting the recognition of South Asian languages in Singapore's educational system.
Singapore's mother-tongue policy is particularly interesting in this respect. Alongside the country's four official mother tongues -- English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay, and Tamil -- students who meet the relevant criteria can study non-Tamil Indian languages, including Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Punjabi, and Urdu.
The principal told me about an encounter he had with Lee Kuan Yew. He explained that he had argued for the importance of allowing children to maintain a connection with their mother tongue. Lee understood the argument and gave his support.
The principal proudly showed me a copy of the letter, now framed and displayed on the wall of his office.
The episode stayed with me because it illustrated something larger than language policy. A country's development is not simply a matter of GDP, technology, or infrastructure. It is also about whether its leaders understand the importance of education, culture, language, and human dignity.
Travel in the global age may no longer give us the same sense of discovering an unknown world that it once did.
Before the internet, arriving in a distant country could mean entering a world about which we knew very little. Today, Google, YouTube, social media, and satellite television have brought much of the world into our living rooms.
But travel has not become irrelevant. Quite the opposite.
Travel allows us to test what we think we know against what actually exists. It introduces us to people whose lives cannot be reduced to statistics.
It allows us to see institutions at work rather than merely read about them. And occasionally, it offers an insight that is difficult to obtain from books or screens.
In Zadar, the sea itself became an orchestra.
In Croatia, I saw how a small country takes education and sport seriously.
Among Bangladeshi migrants, I was reminded of the distance that can exist between a country's citizens and the people who govern them.
In Australia, I saw how democratic institutions and a welfare state can become part of everyday life.
And in Singapore, I was reminded of the transformative possibilities of education and leadership.
Perhaps, then, the real purpose of travel is not to see places. It is to see societies.
These experiences have left me with one broader thought.
Countries do not develop simply because they possess natural resources, favourable geography, or large populations.
Nor does economic growth automatically produce a just, prosperous, or cohesive society.
Institutions have to be built, maintained, and protected. Schools must function. Public officials must do their jobs. Governments must think beyond the next election. And leaders must understand that public office is a responsibility, not a private entitlement.
Education matters enormously because educated leaders are more likely to understand the complexity of modern societies, appreciate evidence, learn from experience, and recognize the importance of institutions.
But education by itself is not enough. An educated person without integrity can become more dangerous, not less.
Knowledge must be accompanied by honesty, competence, humility, and a commitment to the public good.
The examples I encountered on the road -- from Croatia to Australia to Singapore -- are obviously very different, and none should be romanticized. Every society has its contradictions, inequalities, and failures.
Yet they illustrate a common principle: Development depends not only on resources and policies but on the quality of institutions and the people entrusted with them.
A country needs leaders who are educated enough to understand the world, honest enough to resist corruption, competent enough to turn ideas into institutions, and humble enough to listen to ordinary citizens.
Perhaps that is the most important lesson of travel.
The distance between countries is no longer very great. We can cross it in hours.
But the distance between good governance and bad governance, between competent leadership and incompetence, between public service and self-service, can determine the fate of an entire generation.
And that distance is not measured in kilometres.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Keeping the city clean. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is disconcerting that in Dhaka, a city that generates more than 7,000 tons of waste every day, finding a public bin is still challenging -- a basic gap in public infrastructure that should no longer be acceptable.
The absence of bins makes responsible waste disposal unnecessarily difficult. A pedestrian carrying disposables accumulated through daily activities should not have to walk for kilometres to find somewhere to dispose of them.
While this inconvenience certainly cannot excuse littering, it does highlight the responsibility of the city corporations to provide practical facilities that make good behaviour possible.
There have been attempts before. In 2016, more than 11,000 mini bins were installed across Dhaka, but most disappeared within about a year because of theft and inadequate monitoring.
The fact that the capital is facing essentially the same problem a decade later shows that simply installing bins is not enough.
The current plan by Dhaka South City Corporation to install 2,000 heavier, more durable bins is therefore welcome -- but this time, the authorities must also ensure proper placement, regular maintenance, monitoring, and timely waste collection.
Dhaka North City Corporation, meanwhile, should move quickly to finalize a dedicated roadside-bin program instead of leaving pedestrians without convenient disposal options.
At the same time, public responsibility cannot be overlooked. Bins are useful only when people actually use them, and damaging or stealing public facilities only makes an already difficult problem much worse. Littering should not become the default simply because facilities are inadequate.
Ultimately, this is about more than waste management. Public services should be designed around the everyday needs of citizens, while citizens must also take responsibility for protecting and using those services properly. A cleaner Dhaka will require both.
The city corporations must provide the infrastructure and accountability, and the public must do its part too. Only then can keeping Dhaka clean become a shared responsibility rather than an endless struggle.

item.title: Ensuring the right to healthcare. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain’s declaration that either he or irregularities in hospitals will remain is certainly a strong statement, but the circumstances under which he said so are deeply concerning.
A surprise inspection of Mugda Medical College Hospital was conducted, where the complaints being investigated were unfortunately found to be true -- including that of patients being sent to outside diagnostic centres, despite the hospital having facilities to conduct the required tests.
This is just one example of what is undoubtedly a gross neglect of people's right to healthcare.
Government hospitals are meant to provide accessible healthcare to those who cannot afford expensive private treatment. When patients are directed elsewhere for services that are already available within public facilities, they are not only being made to spend more money, but may also be exposed to unnecessary additional steps and other irregular practices.
The minister also heard complaints about lifts not operating regularly, forcing patients and their relatives to struggle between floors. Such seemingly basic failures can become serious problems for elderly, sick, and disabled patients.
However, impromptu inspections and strong statements can only take us so far. What matters now is what actions are truly taken.
To that end, those responsible for irregularities must be identified and held accountable, while systems should be put in place to ensure such practices cannot simply return once the spotlight moves elsewhere.
This should also be a nationwide effort. If irregularities exist in one government hospital, there is every reason to examine whether similar problems exist elsewhere.
Regular unannounced inspections, transparent complaint mechanisms, proper monitoring of diagnostic services, and consequences for those abusing public facilities can help restore confidence in the system.
Our public hospitals serve millions, often under difficult circumstances. They deserve better management, stronger oversight, and greater accountability.
The minister has made his position clear. Now the health sector needs to see to it that his position is translated into lasting action.

White blazers, pink ties as North Koreans land in Japan for Asian Games. [ dawn ]
item.description:
North Korean athletes wearing white blazers and pink ties were met by pro-Pyongyang supporters waving flags as they began arriving in Japan for the Asian Games on Friday.

More than 100 North Koreans are set to compete in 14 sports at the Games, which take place in Nagoya-Aichi and officially open on September 19.

Nuclear-armed North Korea suspended participation in international sporting competitions during the pandemic but returned at the Asian Games in China in 2023 and also took part in the Paris Olympics.

The smartly dressed men’s football team landed in Osaka on a flight from Beijing at around lunch-time.

North Korea’s flag was prominent on the breast of their immaculate blazers, and they also wore blue trousers and light blue shirts.

They were welcomed by a large group of supporters who sang songs and waved the country’s flag.

The team were presented with bouquets before they boarded a bus and waved from the windows, high-fiving well-wishers.

North Korea’s women’s football team, who have enjoyed stunning international success at youth level, were set to arrive in the evening.

While the Asian Games don’t officially open until next weekend, some events, including football, get under way before then.

The North Korean men open their football campaign against China on September 16.

Their women’s team face Bangladesh on Monday and have been drawn in a group that also includes South Korea, who they will play on September 21.

Japan does not allow North Koreans to enter the country as a sanction for its nuclear and missile development programmes, but exceptions can be made for athletes, said Japan’s chief cabinet secretary Minoru Kihara.

The two countries have no diplomatic relations.

“There are special circumstances warranting an exceptional decision to permit entry,” Kihara said, citing the Games’ aim to foster international exchange.

He reiterated that Japan “in principle prohibits entry by North Korean nationals, and there is no change to this policy”.

A pro-North Korean group in Tokyo has called for people living in Japan to come out and support the athletes.

A video published by Choson Sinbo, a pro-North Korean publication based in Japan, showed students from Korea University explaining how to cheer for teams at the Games.

The smiling students demonstrate chants and songs and urge people to attend events wearing the red of North Korea.
